newsitem.title: HONG KONG: No quick fix for China-U.S. trade troubles.
newsitem.headline: No quick fix for China-U.S. trade troubles.

text.p: China's trade surplus with the United States is likely to grow, with structural and accounting problems expected to cause a headache for Washington in the near future, economists in Hong Kong said.
"The outlook for the Chinese economy and prospects for growth all underpin the U.S. deficit with China," Clive McDonnell, economist with Crosby Securities in Hong Kong, said.
The U.S. current account deficit with China grew by 14.75 percent in July over June to $3.82 billion.

That compares with a 32.93 percent jump in Japan's current account surplus with the United States to $4.31 billion, a figure that put Japan ahead of China as the country holding the highest current account surplus with the United States.
But economists said China would reclaim the top spot.
"Looking at the situation with the Japanese surplus, it picked up... from July, and now it's at the top spot again," said McDonnell. "But I think that's just a one-off."
Dong Tao, economist at Schroders Asia, said that while China's overall trade surplus with the world was trending lower, its surplus with the United States would probably rise.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see China to be on top of U.S. list again," said Dong.
Ironically, the United States itself has largely created the catalyst for the surplus with China.
U.S. investment in China has been a key factor in China's emergence as a major trading nation over the past two decades.

In contrast to Japan, China has encouraged U.S. business in the form of joint ventures, a practice economists say has led China to produce many of the goods that the United States is trying to sell in the country.

"When it comes down to trying to export goods from the U.S. into China, one of the problems is that the goods are already there," said McDonnell. "They have already substituted domestic goods for their own products."
McDonnell said that since U.S. goods were at a perceived saturation point in China, the Chinese government was very reluctant to promote U.S. imports.
"It's sort of a double-whammy," said McDonnell.

Dong Tao expected China's surplus against the United States to continue to rise, but he expected China's trade surplus overall to fall to zero this year after hitting an historic high of $11.7 billion last year.
"I don't think from a trading practice point of view China is particularly conducting an unfair practice," said Dong.
"It just happens that because of the trade structure to the particular country -- the United States, it is in a large surplus."

The United States counts imports from China that are re-exported through Hong Kong as coming directly from China, but records its own exports routed through Hong Kong to China as exports to Hong Kong.
China views exports to the United States via Hong Kong as exports to Hong Kong.
"Technically, this actually exaggerated the trade surplus to a large degree," said Dong.
